Next step
Monte Carlo Simulation — Portfolio Success Rate
What is a Monte Carlo Simulation?

A Monte Carlo simulation runs hundreds of randomized trial projections of your portfolio, each with a different sequence of market returns. Rather than assuming a single average return each year, it models real-world volatility — some years up 20%, others down 15%.

This sim uses your full plan: it accumulates contributions until retirement, then each year adds your after-tax pension, VA, and Social Security and draws the remaining expenses from the portfolio (grossing up taxable withdrawals). The Success Rate is the share of 800 trials in which the portfolio lasts the entire retirement without running out. A rate ≥80% is generally considered robust. The 10th/90th percentile bands bracket the realistic range of outcomes.

BRS trade-offs vs High-3: 10% smaller pension (40% vs 50% at 20 yrs) · DoD matches up to 5% of TSP · Continuation Pay lump sum · COLA−1%/yr until age 62 (then catch-up) — pension loses purchasing power ~18–20 years vs High-3 full COLA from day one · Optional lump sum (25%/50% PV) at retirement in exchange for reduced monthly until age 67.
Enter each scenario's base pay separately — it changes with your paygrade and years of service at that retirement date.
"Stop at age" compares scenarios fairly (same final work age). "For N yrs after" favors later retirement — judge it by freedom years.

ⓘWhat it is: The federal & military retirement plan — like a 401(k) but with the lowest fees anywhere and, under BRS, government matching. Has Roth and Traditional sides.
Who it’s for: Active/reserve service members and federal civilian employees.
Why choose it: Rock-bottom-cost investing, automatic from your paycheck, and free matching money. Penalty-free withdrawals at 59½.

ⓘWhat it is: An employer-sponsored retirement plan funded straight from your paycheck (pre-tax or Roth), usually with an employer match.
Who it’s for: Employees whose company offers one.
Why choose it: Pre-tax contributions cut today's taxes, the match is free money, and it grows tax-deferred. Penalty-free at 59½.

ⓘWhat it is: A personal retirement account funded with after-tax dollars — growth and qualified withdrawals come out completely tax-free.
Who it’s for: Anyone with earned income under the IRS income limits.
Why choose it: Tax-free in retirement, no required minimum distributions, and you can withdraw your contributions anytime penalty-free. Best when you expect higher taxes later.

2026 limit: $7,500/yr ($625/mo), or $8,600 if age 50+. Tax-free growth & withdrawals.
ⓘWhat it is: A savings/investment account paired with a high-deductible health plan (HDHP).
Who it’s for: Anyone enrolled in an HDHP.
Why choose it: The only triple-tax-advantaged account: deductible going in, tax-free growth, and tax-free out for medical costs. After 65 it works like a traditional IRA for anything.
$0$100$250$400
Triple tax-advantaged. 2026 individual limit: $4,300/yr. After 65 acts like traditional IRA.
ⓘWhat it is: A tax-advantaged account for education — grows tax-free for college, K-12, apprenticeships, even student-loan payoff.
Who it’s for: Parents, grandparents, or anyone saving for a student.
Why choose it: Tax-free growth for education, often a state tax deduction, high limits, and leftover funds can now roll into the beneficiary's Roth IRA (limits apply).

ⓘWhat it is: Money invested for a child or dependent — e.g., a custodial UTMA/UGMA account or a brokerage earmarked for them.
Who it’s for: Parents/guardians investing for a child's future beyond just education.
Why choose it: Flexible — usable for anything that benefits the child. Note: a custodial account legally becomes the child's at the age of majority and can reduce financial-aid eligibility.

ⓘWhat it is: A standard investment account with no contribution limits and no early-withdrawal penalties; you pay tax on dividends and realized gains.
Who it’s for: Anyone — especially after maxing tax-advantaged accounts, or for goals before retirement age.
Why choose it: Total flexibility to withdraw anytime, no caps, and favorable long-term capital-gains rates. This is your bridge money before retirement accounts unlock.

ⓘWhat it is: Cash and cash-equivalents — checking, high-yield savings, money market, CDs.
Who it’s for: Everyone — for emergencies and near-term needs.
Why choose it: Safe and instantly available for your emergency fund and short-term goals. Not for long-term growth — it barely keeps up with inflation.

Opportunity Cost shows what each purchase would be worth if invested at your set return rate until age 60. All purchases deduct from liquid (non-TSP) savings. Windfalls reduce your FIRE timeline; expenses extend it.
Click "⚙ cost" on any expense to factor the things sticker price hides: financing interest (rate × term), down payment, taxes & fees, ongoing cost of ownership (insurance, maintenance, fuel/energy, HOA), and resale / trade-in value — giving a true cost and a monthly figure that flows into the Budget balance sheet. Also weigh: paying cash vs. financing while keeping cash invested, depreciation vs. appreciation, whether it replaces an existing expense, and the hit to your emergency fund.

Repair-Risk Range — total cost of ownership across 4,000 luck simulations. A wide bar = unpredictable.
Bar spans the typical range (10th–90th percentile); the line marks the median. The new car's bar is tight while under warranty; the used car's stretches right — that tail is the transmission/engine risk you're weighing.
Recommendation
Depreciation uses a typical retention curve (old cars barely depreciate; new cars drop fast early). Repairs scale with age & mileage and are near-zero under warranty. This can't know your specific used car's history or luck — its real value is showing how far things must go wrong before new wins, and the range of outcomes rather than a false-precise number. Not modeled: your down time's true cost, resale condition, and that a used car frees up capital sooner. Add a dollar value under "New peace-of-mind" for safety tech/warranty to see if it flips the call.

Survivor Benefit vs. Life Insurance — protecting your survivor: a lifetime annuity vs. a lump-sum policy
Survivor Benefit (e.g. SBP)
Life Insurance (term)
Survivor benefit — cost to you (PV)
Survivor benefit — value to survivor (PV)
Life insurance — total premiums (PV)
Life insurance — payout
Recommendation
A survivor annuity (like SBP) pays for life, adjusts with inflation, and can't be outlived — but is taxable and ends at the survivor's death. Term life is a tax-free lump sum the survivor controls, but covers only a fixed window and can lapse. Many plans use both: a survivor annuity for the lifetime floor plus term life over the working years.

One-Time Lump Payments — bonuses, tax refunds, or any extra windfall applied on a specific date
Drop in one-off payments on the dates you expect them. Each one hits its debt on that day, on top of your regular plan — freed minimums keep rolling as usual. Pick a specific debt, or leave it on Auto to attack whatever debt is next in line that day.
Snowball pays the smallest balance first (fast wins); Avalanche targets the highest APR first (least interest); Deadline-Aware clears deferred-interest promos before their date so the retroactive interest never triggers. Freed-up minimums roll into the next debt. Your mortgage is tracked separately on the Mortgage tab; use the Include mortgage toggle above to fold it into this plan or leave it out.
